paragraphs: Medical segmentation datasets can contain very different amounts of useful supervision. Some images have many labeled pixels, while others have few or none. The paper studies this information imbalance as a form of concept shift, where relationships between features and labels vary across subpopulations. Simply reducing the influence of sparsely labeled images can leave their visual information underused.

AdaWAC introduces trainable weights that balance two learning signals separately for each sample: supervised prediction loss and unsupervised consistency across data augmentations. At a saddle point of its objective, the weighting assigns densely labeled samples to supervised learning and sparsely labeled samples to consistency regularization. This gives samples different roles according to the information they provide.

The authors establish a convergence guarantee by expressing the optimization as online mirror descent for a saddle point problem. Experiments across medical segmentation tasks and different UNet-style backbones report better segmentation, sample efficiency, and robustness to concept shift. The contribution is a way to use label-sparse samples productively within robust training.
icml-2023-adaptively-weighted-data-augme.tldr: AdaWAC adaptively assigns supervised and consistency-based learning signals to make better use of medical images with uneven label availability.

paragraphs: Reward-conditioned reinforcement learning asks a policy to act according to a specified amount of future reward, called reward-to-go. This offers a flexible way to control behavior, but requesting a high reward creates two challenges: the model must generalize to that request, and the request itself may fall outside the distribution represented in training.

The paper proposes Bayesian Reparameterized RCRL, a set of modeling biases inspired by Bayes’ theorem. It targets what the authors call RTG Independence: the tendency to treat different reward-to-go inputs as unrelated values. Addressing this tendency removes an identified obstacle to generalization at high reward targets. The framework also supports an adaptive inference method that seeks high total returns while avoiding out-of-distribution reward queries.

On the Gym-Mujoco and Atari offline reinforcement learning benchmarks, the authors report state-of-the-art performance and improvements over vanilla reward-conditioned learning of up to 11%. These results support addressing both how reward targets are represented during training and how they are selected during inference.
icml-2023-bayesian-reparameterization-of.tldr: BR-RCRL uses Bayesian-inspired structure and adaptive reward queries to improve reward-conditioned policies on offline reinforcement learning benchmarks.

paragraphs: Few-shot hypothesis adaptation starts with a well-trained classifier from a source domain and only a small labeled dataset from a target domain. Generated unlabeled examples can provide additional information for adapting the classifier. However, the paper identifies a weakness in existing approaches: generated examples can be extremely similar or even identical, making the extra data strongly dependent.

DEG-Net addresses this problem by explicitly encouraging diversity among generated examples. It uses the Hilbert-Schmidt independence criterion, a kernel-based measure of dependence, on the examples’ semantic features. Minimizing this measure encourages independence in those features. The objective therefore targets diversity in the generated data’s semantic representation, rather than merely increasing the number of available examples.

The authors report that DEG-Net produces more diverse and more useful unlabeled data, and outperforms existing few-shot hypothesis adaptation baselines in their experiments. The findings support the role of generated-data diversity in adaptation: additional examples help when they provide varied information, while repeated or highly dependent examples can undermine learning.
icml-2023-diversity-enhancing-generative.tldr: DEG-Net encourages semantic independence among generated examples to improve classifier adaptation with few labeled target-domain samples.

paragraphs: Federated learning requires communication in both directions: clients receive model parameters from a server and send model updates back. Many compression methods focus on updates, whose size in value is expected to shrink during training. The paper explains why techniques built around that behavior do not directly address sending full model parameters to participating devices.

This distinction matters in cross-device learning, where clients are heterogeneous and may participate only once. Such clients still need to download the model, so reducing the cost of outgoing updates leaves a separate communication burden. DoCoFL is a framework designed specifically to compress this server-to-client transfer. It can also be combined with many existing methods for compressing client-to-server updates.

The authors evaluate the combined communication savings and report substantial bandwidth reductions in both directions, with accuracy competitive with an uncompressed baseline. The finding is empirical rather than a claim of identical accuracy in every setting. DoCoFL’s contribution is to make downlink compression a compatible part of a broader federated communication strategy.
icml-2023-docofl-downlink-compression-fo.tldr: DoCoFL compresses server-to-device model downloads and combines with uplink compression to reduce federated learning bandwidth while retaining competitive accuracy.

paragraphs: A misspecified linear bandit provides features that approximate action rewards but leave a uniform error of epsilon. The paper asks whether sparsity in the underlying parameter makes finding a good action easier. Without such structure, prior results require exponentially many queries in feature dimension d for O(epsilon) accuracy, while polynomially many queries permit a weaker O(epsilon times square root of d) guarantee.

The authors show that sparsity changes this dependence. When m measures sparsity, an O(epsilon)-optimal action can be obtained with a query bound that, suppressing logarithmic factors, scales as exp(m epsilon). This removes the exponential dependence on the full dimension, although it does not make the general query requirement polynomial in sparsity.

An information-theoretic lower bound establishes the stated optimality of this tradeoff when the requested error is m to the power delta times epsilon, for delta between zero and one. Polynomial bounds in m/epsilon become possible when the features satisfy the paper’s additional “good” feature condition. Thus, sparsity helps, and feature quality further determines the achievable efficiency.
icml-2023-does-sparsity-help-in-learning.tldr: Sparsity removes exponential dependence on full feature dimension in misspecified bandits, while polynomial query bounds require additional feature structure.

paragraphs: Decentralized stochastic gradient descent lets multiple agents train together without a central parameter server. Each agent maintains model parameters and exchanges updates with a small set of peers. The communication pattern and the weights used to combine messages affect how efficiently information spreads, making communication design part of the optimization problem.

A strong existing approach uses a changing one-peer exponential-2 topology, but requires the number of agents to be a power of two. DSGD-CECA removes that restriction by incorporating a communication-optimal exact consensus algorithm. It supports any number of agents while retaining the stated favorable communication and convergence properties, making the method applicable beyond specially sized groups.

The paper proves unit communication overhead per iteration and a transient iteration complexity of order n cubed, up to logarithmic factors. Its analysis uses newly identified properties of gossip weight matrices and integrates them into decentralized SGD convergence arguments. Numerical experiments support the method’s efficiency. The contribution combines flexible agent counts with theoretical control of communication and training behavior.
icml-2023-dsgd-ceca-decentralized-sgd-wi.tldr: DSGD-CECA enables efficient decentralized training for any number of agents while preserving strong communication and convergence properties.

paragraphs: A general instruction such as defeating all enemies leaves a multi-agent system with several decisions: which entities matter, how to divide the instruction into subgoals, and which subgoal each agent should pursue. As the number of entities grows, grounding language in possible interactions becomes harder. Each agent must also account for the behavior of its teammates.

The proposed Entity Divider framework, EnDi, organizes this learning around entities. Agents independently learn how to divide instructions into entity-level subgoals, then act based on their associated entities. Agent modeling regularizes this division to discourage conflicting subgoals and encourage coordinated strategies. This connects instruction interpretation to both the objects involved and the other agents’ behavior.

Experiments report strong generalization to unseen games with new dynamics and better performance than existing methods. These findings support entity-level subgoal division as a useful structure for language-guided multi-agent learning. The stated evidence concerns generalization in the evaluated games, where successful instruction following requires agents to coordinate their choices as well as understand the language.
icml-2023-entity-divider-with-language-g.tldr: EnDi grounds instructions in entity-level subgoals and uses agent modeling to encourage coordination and generalization to unseen games.

paragraphs: Gaussian variational inference approximates a target probability distribution with a Gaussian distribution. The optimization chooses the Gaussian that minimizes Kullback-Leibler divergence to the target. This paper develops deterministic and stochastic versions of Forward-Backward Gaussian Variational Inference, using the geometry of the space of Gaussian distributions to organize that optimization.

The central observation is that the objective has two components: a smooth potential term and a nonsmooth entropy term. The method treats this composite structure within Bures-Wasserstein space, where distances between Gaussians are measured using Wasserstein distance. Splitting the objective this way provides the basis for a forward-backward algorithm adapted to the distributional optimization problem.

The convergence results depend on the target’s properties. For targets that are both log-smooth and log-concave, the authors obtain state-of-the-art guarantees. With log-smoothness alone, they establish what they describe as the first guarantees of convergence to first-order stationary solutions. That latter result concerns stationarity, so it does not claim that every such solution is a globally best Gaussian approximation.
icml-2023-forward-backward-gaussian-vari.tldr: FB-GVI uses Wasserstein geometry and a split KL objective to obtain Gaussian variational inference guarantees under different target-distribution assumptions.

paragraphs: Graph generative models must represent a large space of possible structures. That output space can make generation expensive and make the underlying distribution harder to model accurately. This paper starts from the observation that many real-world graphs have low graph bandwidth and uses that structural property to reduce the output space considered by existing generators.

The proposed strategy restricts graph bandwidth during both training and generation. The authors report that this improves scalability and generation quality without increasing architectural complexity or reducing expressiveness. They describe how the same strategy applies to autoregressive models, which generate through successive decisions, and one-shot models, showing that the idea is compatible with different generation approaches.

Experiments cover synthetic and real datasets, including molecular graphs. Across these evaluations, bandwidth restriction consistently improves generation quality and reconstruction accuracy, alongside generation efficiency. The significance is that a structural property of the graphs can guide a more manageable output representation, allowing existing generative methods to improve without requiring a more elaborate architecture.
icml-2023-improving-graph-generation-by-.tldr: Restricting graph bandwidth reduces generative output spaces and improves efficiency, quality, and reconstruction in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning a linear decision boundary when the input vectors follow a standard Gaussian distribution but their binary labels can be arbitrary. The learner aims to produce predictions whose classification error is at most epsilon above the error of the best-fitting halfspace. This is an agnostic task: the labels need not follow a perfect linear rule.

The authors establish a near-optimal computational hardness result under the widely believed assumption that Learning with Errors remains hard in sub-exponential time. The result is therefore conditional on a cryptographic hardness assumption. It addresses computational difficulty even with a specifically structured input distribution, rather than relying on unrestricted or irregular input vectors.

Previous hardness results were either qualitatively weaker or limited to restricted algorithm families. The paper strengthens this picture and extends its techniques to related problems, including ReLU regression. Its contribution is to clarify the computational barriers to approaching the best achievable prediction error, with near-optimal lower bounds rather than a new learning algorithm.
icml-2023-near-optimal-cryptographic-har.tldr: Under a Learning with Errors hardness assumption, the paper proves near-optimal computational barriers for agnostic halfspace learning and related ReLU regression.

paragraphs: Principal component analysis seeks a direction along which a distribution has nearly the largest possible variance. Standard estimators can fail badly when even a small fraction of the observations are outliers. Robust PCA addresses this vulnerability by trying to recover a useful high-variance direction despite contamination in the observed dataset.

The paper’s main contribution is an algorithm that combines nearly linear running time with near-optimal error guarantees. This addresses a tradeoff in earlier efficient methods, which either required super-linear time or provided weaker accuracy guarantees. The result concerns both computational cost and robustness: obtaining stronger protection against outliers does not require the same runtime penalty as those earlier approaches.

The authors also develop a single-pass streaming algorithm whose memory usage is nearly linear in the data dimension. This separately addresses the cost of storing and revisiting observations. Together, the results make robust PCA more computationally accessible in two settings: processing an available dataset quickly and processing a stream with limited memory.
icml-2023-nearly-linear-time-and-streami.tldr: The paper gives nearly linear-time robust PCA with near-optimal error and a single-pass streaming method using nearly dimension-linear memory.

paragraphs: The stochastic shortest path problem asks an agent to reach a goal while minimizing accumulated cost in an uncertain environment. This paper studies repeated episodes when transitions have a linear mixture structure. Earlier approaches often require either a strictly positive minimum cost or a bound on the optimal policy’s expected episode length; the proposed algorithm removes those requirements.

The method combines extended value iteration with confidence sets that account carefully for variance. It estimates variance recursively using higher-order moments. This uncertainty treatment is central to the algorithm’s ability to obtain its guarantee without the two restrictive assumptions identified in earlier work.

The regret bound scales as d times B-star times the square root of K, up to logarithmic factors. Here d is the transition-feature dimension, B-star bounds the optimal policy’s cumulative cost, and K counts episodes. Regret measures the excess cost associated with learning. The bound matches the stated lower bound apart from logarithmic factors, supporting the claim of nearly minimax-optimal performance for this problem class.
icml-2023-nearly-minimax-optimal-regret-.tldr: A variance-aware algorithm achieves nearly minimax-optimal regret for linear mixture shortest-path learning without minimum-cost or optimal-episode-length assumptions.

paragraphs: The geometric organization of data can guide machine learning, but this paper asks how that organization relates to a causal model of the data. It characterizes the data manifolds implied by structural causal models. The aim is to give the geometry a causal basis, connecting the shape of the data to the relationships specified by the model.

The resulting framework supports reasoning about the manifold under interventions and counterfactuals. These capabilities connect geometric questions about data to causal questions about changes in the modeled system. Its two stated strengths are therefore linked: the causal model informs the manifold’s structure, and that structure becomes a setting in which causal reasoning can be performed.

The authors illustrate the framework through counterfactual explanations for machine learning classifiers. They generate causally grounded explanations while measuring distances along the data manifold using differential-geometric principles. This application brings together the causal grounding of a proposed counterfactual and a geometric way to quantify its distance, showing how the framework can inform classifier explanations.
icml-2023-on-data-manifolds-entailed-by-.tldr: The paper derives causally informed data geometry from structural causal models and applies it to manifold-based counterfactual explanations.

paragraphs: Message passing neural networks update graph nodes by exchanging information along edges. Over-squashing occurs when a node’s representation becomes insensitive to information at distant nodes. This theoretical paper separates the roles of network width, depth, and graph topology to explain why that loss of influence happens and which changes can address it.

The analysis shows that greater width can mitigate over-squashing, but increases the sensitivity of the whole network. Increasing depth does not resolve the issue in the analysis: as layers are added, vanishing gradients come to dominate over-squashing. These results distinguish the effects of giving messages more representational capacity from simply extending the sequence of message-passing operations.

Graph topology has the greatest role in the authors’ account. They connect over-squashing to pairs of nodes with high commute time, relating the problem to the graph’s connectivity. The framework unifies the study of several mitigation methods and provides theoretical justification for a class of graph-rewiring approaches, which address information flow by changing graph connections.
icml-2023-on-over-squashing-in-message-p.tldr: The analysis connects over-squashing primarily to graph topology, showing that width has a sensitivity cost and added depth cannot resolve it.

paragraphs: Open-vocabulary universal image segmentation aims to label image regions using categories supplied as text at inference time. It encompasses semantic labeling, identifying individual object instances, and panoptic segmentation, which combines background labels with foreground instances. The paper investigates how pretrained CLIP models can support this range of outputs and text-defined categories.

The authors first construct a baseline that directly uses pretrained CLIP without finetuning or distillation. They then introduce MaskCLIP, whose visual encoder integrates mask tokens into a pretrained vision-transformer CLIP model. This encoder-only module supports segmentation and class prediction by learning to use CLIP’s partial and dense features. It avoids a time-consuming student-teacher training process.

MaskCLIP outperforms previous methods on semantic, instance, and panoptic segmentation evaluations using ADE20K and PASCAL datasets. Qualitative illustrations also show outputs for custom categories supplied online. The contribution is a way to adapt pretrained visual-language features to region-level predictions across multiple segmentation tasks, with reported benchmark improvements and demonstrations of flexible category specification.
icml-2023-open-vocabulary-universal-imag.tldr: MaskCLIP integrates mask tokens with pretrained CLIP features to perform multiple segmentation tasks using text-defined categories.

paragraphs: Tasks trained together can compete, so improving one task may reduce performance on another. Multi-task learning therefore often involves selecting among tradeoffs rather than finding a single solution that is best for every task. The paper focuses on learning a continuous Pareto front, allowing users to adjust those tradeoffs instead of receiving one fixed solution or several discrete choices.

The authors conjecture that the Pareto front admits a linear parameterization in model parameter space. This motivates Pareto Manifold Learning, which ensembles single-task models in weight space. The approach produces a continuous front in one training run and allows task performance to be modulated during inference. The proposed linear structure is presented as a conjecture, rather than a universal theorem.

Experiments span image classification, tabular data, and scene understanding. The method outperforms state-of-the-art single-point algorithms and learns a better Pareto parameterization than the evaluated multi-point baselines. These results support weight-space ensembling as a practical way to expose adjustable task tradeoffs without separately training each desired operating point.
icml-2023-pareto-manifold-learning-tackl.tldr: Pareto Manifold Learning ensembles model weights to learn continuous, inference-time-adjustable task tradeoffs in a single training run.

paragraphs: Assortment optimization chooses which products to offer to customers. In the offline setting studied here, a firm has historical records of offered assortments, customer choices, and revenue, but does not know the underlying choice model. Because there are many possible product combinations, the historical data may cover only a limited part of the decision space.

PASTA applies the principle of pessimism to this incomplete-data problem. The authors show that, under general settings, it can correctly identify the optimal assortment while requiring data coverage of that assortment, rather than coverage of every possible assortment. The coverage condition is central: the result describes what can be learned when the historical data support the optimal choice.

The paper establishes the first stated regret bound for offline assortment optimization under a multinomial logit choice model. It also supplies an efficient computational procedure for solving the pessimistic optimization problem. Numerical studies show better performance than the existing baseline, combining a theoretical account of limited coverage with a computationally usable approach.
icml-2023-pasta-pessimistic-assortment-o.tldr: PASTA uses pessimistic offline optimization to learn assortments with guarantees that require coverage of the optimal assortment.

paragraphs: Guided diffusion sampling introduces conditional information into image generation, allowing the output to respond to a requested condition. However, guidance creates a tradeoff among image quality, diversity, and adherence to that condition. This paper studies that tradeoff by reinterpreting the sampling process as a sequence of optimization updates to the image itself.

In the PixelAsParam view, pixels are the parameters being optimized, and each mathematical term in the sampling procedure supplies an update direction. This exposes conflicts between directions that would otherwise appear as separate parts of a denoising formula. The authors investigate these conflicts and propose a simple projection method to address them during sampling.

Experiments report improvements over different baselines on datasets with varied image resolutions. The results support the usefulness of examining how sampling updates interact, rather than considering each contribution in isolation. The paper’s central contribution is both an interpretation of guided sampling and a concrete adjustment motivated by that interpretation; it does not claim that all quality-diversity-conditioning tradeoffs disappear.
icml-2023-pixelasparam-a-gradient-view-o.tldr: PixelAsParam treats guided diffusion as pixel optimization and uses projection to address conflicting update directions.

paragraphs: Gradient methods can be slowed by poorly conditioned optimization problems, where the relevant eigenvalues are unevenly distributed. This paper studies preconditioning for structured convex problems: modifying the optimization geometry to make first-order methods more effective. It proposes a family of preconditioners constructed using symmetric polynomials.

The preconditioners provably improve the condition number by narrowing gaps between the largest eigenvalues, without explicitly knowing the actual spectrum. The authors give a stochastic interpretation through coordinate volume sampling and compare the construction with classical approaches, including Chebyshev polynomials. They incorporate it into both Gradient and Fast Gradient methods and establish improved global complexity bounds.

The paper also proposes an adaptive search procedure for the Gradient Method. It minimizes the objective over a low-dimensional Krylov subspace to automatically obtain the best polynomial preconditioning described by the approach. Numerical experiments on machine learning problems support its efficiency. Together, the results connect a theoretically motivated preconditioner family with a practical way to select preconditioning during optimization.
icml-2023-polynomial-preconditioning-for.tldr: Symmetric-polynomial preconditioners improve gradient-method conditioning and complexity without explicit knowledge of the problem’s spectrum.

paragraphs: Newton-style optimization uses gradients and Hessians, with the Hessian supplying second-order information about the objective. This paper asks how often that second-order information must be refreshed. Its method reuses a previously computed Hessian across several iterations while computing a new gradient at every step, reducing the arithmetic work associated with second-order optimization.

For general, possibly nonconvex problems, cubic regularization gives fast global convergence to a second-order stationary point despite the delayed Hessian updates. This is a stationarity guarantee rather than a guarantee of finding a global minimum. For convex problems, the authors justify global convergence and local superlinear rates using quadratic regularization, which is easier to compute.

The analysis identifies updating the Hessian once every d iterations as the optimal frequency, where d is the problem dimension. This yields a provable square-root-of-d improvement in total arithmetic complexity. The result shows that carefully controlled reuse of curvature information can preserve strong convergence properties while reducing the overall computational cost of the method.
icml-2023-second-order-optimization-with.tldr: Reusing Hessians for multiple Newton steps preserves stated convergence guarantees and improves arithmetic complexity by a square-root-of-dimension factor.

paragraphs: Reducing a detector’s computation does not necessarily produce a matching reduction in runtime. The paper argues that transformer-based object detectors also depend on memory access costs and the degree of parallelism available on the hardware. Designs focused only on computation can therefore miss practical speed improvements, especially on multicore processors such as GPUs.

SpeedDETR uses a latency prediction model to guide architecture design. The predictor analyzes network properties, hardware memory access patterns, and parallelism to estimate runtime directly. Combined with a local-to-global visual modeling process, this guidance produces a family of hardware-oriented transformer detectors. The design objective is connected to actual inference latency rather than computation counts alone.

Experiments on MS COCO report that SpeedDETR outperforms current DETR-based methods on Tesla V100 hardware. The authors also report acceptable inference speed on edge GPUs and high-speed inference across multiple devices. These findings support accounting for hardware behavior during model design, with the reported evidence tied to the evaluated detectors and devices.
icml-2023-speeddetr-speed-aware-transfor.tldr: SpeedDETR designs transformer detectors around predicted hardware latency, accounting for memory access and parallelism as well as computation.

paragraphs: This paper asks what it means for a differentially private estimator to perform optimally on each individual dataset. It introduces a benchmark that already knows the dataset and is judged by its worst-case performance over large subsets of that dataset. A single private algorithm must compete with this benchmark simultaneously for every dataset.

The benchmark must tolerate removal of a small number of existing points, but need not perform well after potentially extreme new points are added. That narrower evaluation requirement makes the benchmark stronger than earlier alternatives: it has fewer situations to handle. The challenge is to match this demanding dataset-specific comparator while retaining differential privacy.

For real-valued datasets, the authors construct algorithms achieving this notion of instance optimality for properties including means, quantiles, and minimizers of l-p norms. Their detailed mean-estimation analysis shows asymptotic performance matching or exceeding existing algorithms across a range of distributional assumptions. The contribution links a stronger definition of adaptation to concrete private estimation procedures.
icml-2023-subset-based-instance-optimali.tldr: The paper defines a stronger subset-based benchmark for private estimation and constructs algorithms that meet it for several dataset properties.

paragraphs: Automated robot design searches for bodies that can be controlled effectively and perform tasks efficiently. The paper argues that searching directly through a vast design space while ignoring common structures can produce unusual robot forms and poor performance. It proposes using symmetry to organize the design process and make that search more effective.

The Symmetry-Aware Robot Design framework represents symmetries through subgroups of the dihedral group. It searches these structured subgroups for an appropriate symmetry, then designs a robot under the selected symmetry. This separates the choice of structural organization from the subsequent body design. The authors theoretically analyze how the framework can produce efficient symmetric robots while still covering the original design space.

Experiments across various tasks report superior efficiency and generalizability. These results support incorporating structural search into robot design rather than treating every body configuration as an unrelated possibility. The theoretical coverage claim also matters: in the authors’ framework, introducing symmetry into the search does not require giving up coverage of the original design space.
icml-2023-symmetry-aware-robot-design-wi.tldr: SARD searches over symmetry structures before designing robot bodies, improving reported efficiency and generalization while retaining design-space coverage.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks rely on connections to pass information between nodes, so structural problems in a graph can impair learning. This paper addresses both measuring such noise and reducing its effect. Its starting point is that edge quality should be assessed relative to the data’s features or labels, rather than considering graph structure alone.

The authors propose edge signal-to-noise ratio, or ESNR, using random matrix theory to evaluate the overall level of edge noise. They find strong agreement between this metric and GNN performance on simulated and real data. This provides evidence that the measure captures a structural property relevant to learning, though the reported agreement is an empirical finding.

To improve the graph, the paper introduces Graph Propensity Score rewiring. GPS estimates edge likelihoods through self-supervised link prediction and uses those estimates to rewire the data graph. The authors provide a theoretical guarantee and benchmark evidence for the method. The combined contribution supplies a diagnostic measure and a learning-based approach to changing noisy connections.
icml-2023-towards-understanding-and-redu.tldr: The paper measures graph edge noise with ESNR and reduces its effects through self-supervised, likelihood-based GPS rewiring.

paragraphs: ELECTRA-style pretraining depends sensitively on the size of its auxiliary generator, making model selection costly through trial and error. This paper systematically studies that sensitivity. Its theoretical investigation identifies control of generator capacity as important and argues that the original optimization design does not manage generator training effectively.

The authors trace the problem to joint optimization with adaptive optimizers such as Adam. In this setting, assigning weights to individual losses does not provide the intended control over their optimization. The proposed change fully separates the generator optimizer from the discriminator optimizer, replacing reliance on a weighted combination of objectives with independently managed optimization.

The resulting technique substantially reduces training sensitivity and produces considerable performance gains over the original design in the reported results. Its significance is that the problem is addressed through how the components are optimized, rather than only through repeated searches for a generator size. The paper connects an analysis of lost optimization control to a simple modular change that restores it.
icml-2023-understand-and-modularize-gene.tldr: Separating generator and discriminator optimizers reduces ELECTRA’s sensitivity to generator selection and improves reported pretraining performance.
